blocks.x: Biochemistry is simply the chemistry of living things. Every cell in your body — and in every plant, animal, and bacterium on earth — is really just a very organized bag of chemical reactions.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — your body as a kitchen

blocks.x: Imagine your body is a busy kitchen that never closes. Food comes in as raw ingredients (rice, cassava, meat, oil). Biochemistry is the study of exactly what happens to those ingredients once they enter the kitchen — how they're chopped, cooked, combined, stored, or turned into waste. Nothing "magical" happens; it's all traceable chemical reactions, just like a recipe is a traceable series of steps.

Because biochemistry looks at life at the chemical and molecular level, it overlaps heavily with Cell biology, Molecular biology, Immunology, and Molecular genetics. Most of biochemistry is about four big families of molecules: proteins, nucleic acids, carbohydrates, and lipids — and how cells harness energy from the environment through chemical reactions collectively called metabolism.

sections.title: Where did the word come from?

blocks.x: The term "Biochemistry" was coined in 1903 by German chemist Carl Neuberg, from the Greek word "bios" meaning life. But the discoveries that built the field stretch back over 250 years — like a relay race where each scientist ran their leg and passed the baton forward.
Biochemistry now underlies medicine, agriculture, veterinary science, biotechnology, and genetics — anywhere the goal is to understand or fix living systems at the molecular level.

<term d="The sum of all chemical reactions that convert food nutrients into energy and into the complex molecules cells are built from.">Metabolism</term> is the sum of all chemical changes that convert food into usable energy and into the complex materials your cells are made of. It's not one reaction — it's a whole coordinated network of thousands of reactions, organized into discrete pathways, each one run by specific <term d="Proteins that speed up (catalyze) specific chemical reactions without being consumed themselves.">enzymes</term>.

Think of your body like a household managing money and supplies. Living organisms need continuous energy for three jobs: (1) physical work — like a person doing manual labour; (2) building things — like buying materials to build an extension to the house; and (3) moving goods around — like transporting items in and out of a locked store room (this is exactly what happens when cells actively move molecules across membranes). To survive, every household (cell) must do two things: make what it needs that isn't supplied from outside, and protect itself from harmful things coming in from outside.

To meet these needs, the body runs four broad types of pathways: fuel oxidative pathways (burning fuel for energy), fuel storage and mobilization pathways (like a granary, storing food for later and releasing it when needed), biosynthetic pathways (building new materials), and detoxification/waste disposal pathways (like a proper waste management system that clears out toxins before they cause harm).
Every metabolic pathway moves in one of two directions — and a few special ones sit right at the crossroads of both.

blocks.x: Catabolism is like a demolition team knocking down an old building — big structures broken into smaller rubble, and in the process, resources (and here, energy) get freed up. Anabolism is the construction crew on the next plot, using materials (and energy, mostly from ATP) to build something new from smaller units — bricks into walls, walls into a house. Anabolism happens in three stages: making the simple building blocks, "activating" them using ATP energy (like prepping cement by mixing it with water before use), then assembling them into the finished structure.

Picture a busy roundabout in town that traffic from a demolition site AND traffic from a construction site both pass through. That's an <term d="A metabolic pathway that plays a role in both catabolism (breaking down) and anabolism (building up).">amphibolic pathway</term> — most famously the <term d="Also called the Krebs Cycle; a central, cyclic pathway that both releases energy from fuels and supplies building blocks for biosynthesis.">Citric Acid Cycle</term> (Krebs Cycle). It doesn't belong purely to demolition or construction — it links both.

Enzyme deficiencies can disrupt any of these pathways. When a genetic defect knocks out a specific enzyme, it's called an <term d="A genetic condition where a missing or faulty enzyme disrupts a specific metabolic pathway, causing abnormal build-up or shortage of certain molecules.">inborn error of metabolism</term> — like one broken machine on an assembly line causing a pile-up of unfinished parts behind it.

sections.title: Why do humans, plants, and bacteria run on the same "software"?

blocks.x: Despite there being more than 10 million species on Earth, the core biochemistry inside their cells is strikingly similar — the same major pathways show up again and again.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — every smartphone runs on similar electronics

blocks.x: It's a bit like how an iPhone, a Samsung, and a Tecno phone all look completely different on the outside, but inside, they all rely on the same basic electronic principles — a battery, a processor, a circuit board. Life is similar: whether it's a human, a mango tree, or a bacterium, the same core "circuitry" — cell membranes, similar metabolic routes, similar chemical building blocks — is being reused. This is strong evidence that all life descended from a common ancestor.

Across organisms, cells share common themes: they maintain specific internal concentrations of ions and molecules, use their outer membrane as a physical barrier separating "inside" from "outside," extract energy from external sources to power reactions that need energy, and follow instructions for their metabolic pathways written into their genes.

sections.title: How are the enzymes in a pathway arranged?

blocks.x: A metabolic pathway is a sequence of steps, but the enzymes running those steps can be organized in three different ways.

Each step is catalyzed by its own free-floating enzyme, with its own specific substrate, and each pathway can be regulated independently. Analogy: like separate roadside food vendors along a street — each sells one specific dish, works independently, and can raise or lower their own prices without asking the others. Examples: Glycolysis, the Pentose Phosphate Pathway, and fatty acid synthesis.

Several enzymes are physically clustered together, passing intermediates directly from one to the next — called channeling — for speed and efficiency, with less product lost along the way. Analogy: like a well-drilled kitchen team where the person chopping vegetables hands them straight to the person frying, who hands the finished dish straight to the person plating — nothing sits around getting cold or going missing.

Enzymes are attached to or embedded within a membrane (cell membrane or organelle membrane) — either fully embedded (integral) or stuck to the surface (peripheral). Often involved in signal transduction, transport, or metabolism, e.g. receptor enzymes, transport ATPases, and cytochrome P450 enzymes. Analogy: like security checkpoints built directly into the wall of a compound gate — fixed in place, controlling exactly what crosses in or out.
Zoom out, and metabolic pathways generally take one of three shapes.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — three kinds of journeys

blocks.x: A Linear pathway is like a straight trotro route from Kejetia to Adum — one stop's passengers become the next stop's starting point, moving in one direction only. A Cyclic pathway is like a roundabout route — the same "stops" (intermediates) get regenerated every time you go around, over and over. A Spiral pathway is like reusing the exact same small tool repeatedly to add one more link to a growing chain — the same set of enzymes is used again and again, just extending the product a little further each pass, such as when fatty acid chains are lengthened.

Pathways are tightly regulated so the organism can respond quickly to changing conditions — most regulatory responses happen within milliseconds. Importantly, most metabolic pathways are irreversible under normal physiological conditions, and metabolic pathways are generally not at equilibrium — reactants and products are always shifting, not sitting still.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — a busy market's supply chain

blocks.x: Think of a metabolic pathway like the flow of tomatoes from farm to market stall. If the pathway were "at equilibrium," it would mean tomatoes are piling up equally at every stage with nothing moving — clearly not how a working market behaves. Instead, there's constant <term d="The rate of flow of material through a metabolic pathway — how fast substrates are being converted into products.">flux</term> — tomatoes are always flowing from farm, to transport, to market, to your kitchen — and at any stage, a bottleneck (a regulated enzyme) can be tightened or loosened almost instantly to control how much moves through.

sections.title: Gibbs Free Energy — the "will it run on its own?" test

blocks.x: Gibbs Free Energy (ΔG) is the maximum useful energy a reaction can release, and it predicts whether that reaction will happen on its own or not. It's calculated as: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, where ΔH is the enthalpy change, T is temperature, and ΔS is the entropy change.
Energy-releasing, thermodynamically favourable, and spontaneous — it proceeds forward on its own. Analogy: like water flowing downhill on its own — no push needed.
Requires an input of energy to proceed; not thermodynamically favourable on its own. Analogy: like pushing a loaded wheelbarrow uphill — it won't move unless you supply the effort.

No net change in the concentration of reactants and products — the system has reached balance. Analogy: like a seesaw perfectly balanced — movement in both directions is still happening, but there's no net shift either way.

Cells don't spend raw food energy directly. Instead, they convert it into a handful of special molecules called <term d="Activated molecules carrying high-energy bonds that release large amounts of usable energy when broken (hydrolyzed).">energy currencies</term> — think of these as different denominations of cash the cell keeps on hand to "pay" for reactions.

blocks.title: Everyday scenario — Mobile Money vs. cash vs. cheque

blocks.x: <term d="Adenosine triphosphate — the primary energy currency of the cell.">ATP</term> is like Mobile Money — the fast, universal, everyday currency used for almost every transaction. When ATP is <term d="Broken down by reaction with water.">hydrolyzed</term>, it becomes ADP plus a phosphate group, releasing energy that gets used to "phosphorylate" (attach a phosphate to) another molecule — like transferring credit from your wallet to pay someone directly. <term d="Guanosine triphosphate — an energy-rich molecule mainly used in protein synthesis and signal transduction.">GTP</term> is a more specialised currency, used mainly for particular jobs like protein-building and cell signalling — like a cheque that only certain offices accept. <term d="Electron carrier molecules that transport high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain, where that energy is used to produce large amounts of ATP.">NADH and FADH2</term> aren't spent directly — they're more like carrying a sealed bag of coins to the "central bank" (the electron transport chain), where they get converted into a large batch of spendable ATP.

items: <term d="The science concerned with the chemical basis of life.">Biochemistry</term> is the chemistry behind everything living things do.
Metabolism is the entire network of reactions — catabolism breaks down and releases energy, anabolism builds up and needs energy, and amphibolic pathways sit at the crossroads of both.
Despite huge diversity across life, organisms share a remarkably similar core set of pathways — strong evidence of a shared evolutionary origin.
Pathway enzymes can be arranged as separate systems, multienzyme complexes, or membrane-bound systems, and pathways themselves take a linear, cyclic, or spiral shape.

<term d="A measure predicting whether a reaction happens spontaneously.">Gibbs Free Energy</term> tells us whether a reaction runs on its own (exergonic), needs energy input (endergonic), or has settled into balance (equilibrium).
Cells "pay" for their reactions using energy currencies — mainly ATP, plus GTP, NADH, and FADH2 for more specialised jobs.
When metabolism goes wrong — through genetic defects, dietary deficiency, or disease — it can lead to conditions such as diabetes, obesity, and metabolic syndrome.

lines: "Cata-DOWN, Ana-UP" — CATAbolism breaks things DOWN (releases energy); ANAbolism builds things UP (uses energy).
"Line, Circle, Spring" — Linear pathways go straight, Cyclic pathways go in a circle, Spiral pathways coil round and round reusing the same enzymes (like a spring).
"AMPHIbolic = AMPHIbious" — just like an amphibian lives in two worlds (land + water), an amphibolic pathway lives in two roles (catabolic + anabolic).
Amphibolic = serves BOTH roles (e.g. Krebs cycle)
GTP also used, esp. in protein synthesis & signaling
Spiral — e.g. fatty acid synthesis (same enzymes reused)

items.d: Carbohydrates, fats, and proteins enter the body from food.
Large molecules are broken down into smaller units, releasing energy (exergonic) as ATP, NADH, and FADH2.
Breakdown products converge into shared intermediates like acetyl-CoA and pyruvate.
Released energy is captured in ATP and reduced coenzymes (NADH, FADH2) for use elsewhere in the cell.
Using that captured energy, the cell builds larger molecules (proteins, lipids, nucleic acids) from smaller building blocks.
Pathways like the Krebs cycle sit at the crossroads, supporting both catabolic energy release and anabolic biosynthesis.
